questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: Shown a photograph of a crowd and asked to count how many people are visibly angry, most people report a higher count than a careful frame-by-frame analysis actually supports. The bias runs in a predictable direction: negative expressions are detected faster and remembered more vividly than neutral or positive ones, a pattern researchers attribute to an evolved threat-detection system that treats a missed angry face as far costlier than a false alarm. The same asymmetry appears in memory for entire days: a single unpleasant interaction can dominate someone's recollection of an otherwise pleasant afternoon, disregarded proportion entirely.

options.text: Why Crowds Appear Larger in Memory Than They Really Are
The Negativity Bias: Why Bad Impressions Outweigh Good Ones
How Threat-Detection Systems Evolved in Early Humans
The Accuracy of Frame-by-Frame Photographic Analysis
Why Unpleasant Interactions Are Rare in Daily Life

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A meeting scheduled for sixty minutes reliably takes close to sixty minutes, even when the actual agenda could be handled in twenty, a pattern often summarised as "work expands to fill the time available for its completion." The effect is not laziness so much as a lack of a forcing constraint: without an externally imposed shorter deadline, discussion naturally expands to occupy whatever slot has been allocated, since there is no cost to continuing and no clear signal that the matter is actually settled. Organisations that impose deliberately shorter default meeting lengths often find the same agendas handled adequately in a fraction of the original time.

options.text: why meetings are the least productive form of workplace communication
how the absence of a shorter externally imposed deadline lets tasks expand to fill available time
techniques for building an effective meeting agenda
the ideal number of participants for a productive meeting
why organisations should eliminate scheduled meetings entirely

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A single beehive can represent the pooled foraging decisions of tens of thousands of individual bees, none of which possesses anything resembling a map of the surrounding landscape, yet the hive collectively identifies and exploits the richest nearby flower patches with striking efficiency. Individual foragers report a patch's quality through the vigour of their waggle dance, and other bees weight their own subsequent foraging decisions according to how many times they observe a particular dance repeated. No single bee compares patches directly; the comparison emerges only at the level of the whole hive, through thousands of small, individually uninformed decisions aggregating into a collectively intelligent outcome.

options.text: the physical mechanics of the waggle dance itself
how collective intelligence about food sources emerges from many individually uninformed decisions
the total foraging range of a typical honeybee colony
why some bees are better foragers than others
methods beekeepers use to relocate a hive to richer feeding grounds

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: A comedian testing new material in front of a small, unfamiliar audience treats the audience's silence very differently from how a novice performer does: where a novice hears silence as failure and abandons the joke, an experienced comedian treats the same silence as data, adjusting timing, wording, or delivery and testing the revised version at the very next show. Over dozens of iterations, jokes that survive have typically been rewritten many times in ways no audience member ever witnesses individually; what looks like a single polished performance is the visible tail end of an unseen, iterative editing process.

options.text: Silence from an audience always indicates that a joke has genuinely failed.
What appears to be a single polished performance is often the end product of many unseen revisions.
Novice performers are generally more skilled at reading audience reactions than experienced comedians.
Comedians should avoid testing new material in front of unfamiliar audiences.
Audience silence is caused primarily by unfamiliarity with the performer.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
When I took over my grandmother's vegetable patch, I assumed more water and more fertiliser would simply produce more vegetables, and I applied both generously all summer. The tomatoes grew tall and leafy and produced almost no fruit at all. A neighbour eventually explained that excess nitrogen pushes a plant to grow foliage at the direct expense of flowering and fruiting, and that my "generous" feeding had been actively working against the harvest I wanted. The following year I fed the same bed far less, watered only when the soil actually felt dry rather than on a fixed schedule, and harvested more tomatoes from half the effort than I had the previous summer.

Statements
(a) The writer initially believed more water and fertiliser would straightforwardly increase her harvest.
(b) Her first summer's tomato plants produced abundant fruit despite excessive feeding.
(c) A neighbour explained that excess nitrogen favours foliage growth over fruiting.
(d) In the second year, she watered according to a fixed schedule rather than the soil's actual condition.
(e) She used less fertiliser in the second year than in the first.
(f) Her second-year harvest was smaller despite requiring more effort.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Deep-sea anglerfish have evolved an unusual reproductive strategy: the tiny male permanently fuses to the far larger female's body, eventually losing his own eyes and internal organs and surviving on nutrients supplied through her bloodstream. One explanation holds that this strategy evolved because mates are so rare in the vast, dark deep sea that a male who finds a female at all cannot risk losing her, and permanent fusion guarantees he will be available when she is ready to spawn. A second, competing explanation emphasises energy efficiency: maintaining an independent male's full metabolism in a food-scarce environment is wasteful, and fusion lets the pair function as a single, more efficiently resourced reproductive unit.

options.text: The first explanation attributes fusion to the rarity of encountering a mate in the deep sea.
The first explanation suggests fusion guarantees a male's availability when the female is ready to spawn.
The second explanation attributes fusion to the energy inefficiency of maintaining two separate metabolisms.
The second explanation agrees with the first that mate scarcity is the primary reason for fusion.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same observed reproductive strategy.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains the meaning of the underlined phrase "choice-supportive bias"?
questions.context: People asked to rate two similarly attractive options before choosing between them, and asked again immediately after choosing, typically rate the option they picked slightly higher and the rejected option slightly lower than they did beforehand, despite nothing about either option having actually changed. Researchers call this _choice-supportive bias_: once a decision is made, memory and evaluation quietly reshape themselves to make the choice already made look like the obviously correct one, reducing the discomfort of having given up a genuinely attractive alternative.

options.text: a tendency to choose options that other people have already chosen
a tendency to retroactively rate a chosen option more favourably than before the choice was made
a preference for options that require the least deliberation to select
the fact that people always regret rejecting an attractive alternative
a bias that only affects decisions made under significant time pressure

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: Naked mole rats live in large underground colonies structured almost like a beehive, with a single breeding queen who suppresses reproduction in all other colony members through both chemical signals and direct aggression, while non-breeding workers dig tunnels, gather food, and defend the colony. Remarkably, naked mole rats appear largely resistant to cancer and show almost no decline in fertility or physical capability with age, living up to eight times longer than similarly sized rodents. Researchers have linked this resilience partly to unusually error-resistant protein synthesis and partly to a highly efficient cellular repair mechanism, though the full picture remains under active investigation.

questions.text: How many of the underlined parts are grammatically INCORRECT?
questions.context: The bystander effect, in which the presence of other witnesses reduces any single person's likelihood of intervening in an emergency, has been documented across dozens of controlled experiments. ① _Researchers staging a fake medical emergency finds that a lone witness intervenes in the overwhelming majority of trials._ ② _Adding several additional passive witnesses to the same staged scene reduce the intervention rate sharply, sometimes to a fraction of the lone-witness figure._ ③ _Each witness, observing the others' inaction, appears to recalculate the emergency as less urgent than it actually is._ ④ _Diffusion of responsibility, rather than simple indifference, is generally offered as the explanation._ ⑤ _Training that explicitly names the bystander effect has been shown to measurably increase intervention rates in subsequent staged emergencies._

questions.text: Which underlined part is grammatically incorrect?
questions.context: Cognitive load theory ① _holds_ that working memory can process only a limited amount of new information at once before performance begins to degrade. Instructional designers ② _have found_ that presenting the same content through both spoken narration and matching on-screen text simultaneously ③ _impose_ an unnecessary burden, since learners attempt to reconcile two channels carrying identical information rather than processing either efficiently. Redundant information of this kind, counterintuitively, often ④ _produces_ worse learning outcomes than a single well-chosen channel alone. Effective instructional design, on this view, ⑤ _removes_ redundancy rather than simply adding more explanatory material.

questions.text: Among the dictionary definitions below, how many describe words that do NOT appear in the passage? (Ignore singular/plural forms, voice, and tense.)
questions.context:
Urban planners studying pedestrian behaviour have found that people rarely walk in perfectly straight lines between two points; instead, foot traffic gradually carves out slightly curved, efficient paths worn into grass verges that planners call desire lines, revealing where people actually want to walk rather than where a paved path was originally laid. Rather than fighting this pattern with fences or repeated reseeding, some planners now deliberately wait a season, observe where desire lines emerge naturally, and then pave precisely along those routes, producing paths pedestrians overwhelmingly prefer to the ones originally designed for them.

Definitions
(a) a path or route created gradually by repeated use rather than deliberate design
(b) to make an area of ground level and hard by covering it with a surface
(c) to plant seeds again in an area where grass has died or been damaged
(d) a barrier used to enclose an area or prevent access to it
(e) to prefer one thing over another available alternative
(f) money paid regularly to support a cause or organisation
(g) a formal request submitted for official approval
(h) the act of measuring the exact boundaries of a piece of land

Chesterton: before removing a fence whose purpose is not immediately obvious, first find out why it was put there in the first place. The principle is not an argument against ever changing an old rule or structure; it is an argument against changing one before understanding it, since a rule that looks pointless to someone unfamiliar with its history may in fact be ________. Only once the original purpose is understood, the principle holds, is a person actually in a position to judge whether the rule is still worth keeping.

options.text: completely pointless and safe to remove without any further investigation
quietly solving a problem that is no longer visible to someone encountering it fresh
something no one has ever benefited from at any point in its history

questions.context: Migratory monarch butterflies travelling from Canada to central Mexico complete a journey no single individual butterfly has ever made before, since the generation that arrives in Mexico is several generations removed from the one that made the outbound journey the previous year. ① No monarch alive at journey's end has any personal memory of the route, since the ones who began it have long since died. ② The navigational information must therefore be inherited rather than learned, encoded somehow in the insect's biology rather than passed down through experience or observation. ③ Monarch caterpillars feed exclusively on milkweed plants, which contain toxins that make the adult butterfly unpalatable to most predators. ④ Researchers suspect a combination of a time-compensated sun compass and sensitivity to the Earth's magnetic field allows each new generation to orient correctly without ever having seen the route before. ⑤ The precision of the destination, often the very same forest groves each year, remains one of the more striking examples of inherited, rather than learned, animal navigation.

[Sentence to insert] Crucially, the correction is rarely permanent, fading back toward the original overconfident estimate within a matter of weeks.
questions.context: Project planners asked to estimate how long a task will take routinely underestimate the actual time required, a pattern so consistent it has its own name: the planning fallacy. ( ① ) Even planners who have personally experienced this exact bias on previous, similar projects continue to underestimate on the next one, suggesting the bias is not simply a lack of relevant experience. ( ② ) One of the few interventions that reliably improves accuracy is asking planners to imagine, in specific detail, everything that could plausibly go wrong before finalising an estimate. ( ③ ) This "premortem" exercise measurably lengthens the resulting estimate and brings it closer to the eventual actual outcome. ( ④ ) Organisations that adopt premortems as a standing practice, rather than a one-off exercise, report more durable improvements in estimate accuracy. ( ⑤ )

questions.text:
Choose the most appropriate place for the given sentence.

[Sentence to insert] This is why a familiar face glimpsed unexpectedly in an unfamiliar setting, such as a colleague encountered on holiday in another country, can take a disorienting extra moment to place.
questions.context: Face recognition, though remarkably fast and accurate under ordinary conditions, depends more heavily on context than most people realise. ( ① ) The brain appears to use expected context as a genuine input to the recognition process itself, not merely as a helpful afterthought once a face has already been identified. ( ② ) Experiments briefly showing familiar faces against an unexpected background context measurably slow recognition time and increase the error rate compared with the same faces shown in an expected setting. ( ③ ) The delay is not a failure of memory for the face itself, since recognition eventually succeeds; it is a failure of the context-matching step that ordinarily happens so quickly it goes unnoticed. ( ④ ) Once the surrounding context is consciously supplied — "of course, that's my colleague" — recognition suddenly resolves. ( ⑤ )

A city's traffic signal timing illustrates how optimising one measurable goal can quietly undermine an unmeasured one.

(A) As a direct result, pedestrians crossing on foot face measurably longer average waiting times at every signal along the corridor, an outcome the original optimisation never measured or accounted for.
(B) Engineers optimising a busy corridor's signal timing for vehicle throughput adjust green-light durations specifically to minimise the average car's delay across the whole corridor.
(C) Only once pedestrian advocacy groups began independently measuring crossing wait times did the trade-off the original optimisation had quietly created become visible to the city at all.

Choose the most appropriate order for the paragraphs following the given passage.

A tropical rainforest canopy hosts an entire ecosystem that never touches the forest floor at all.

(A) Some canopy-dwelling frog species complete their entire life cycle, from egg to adulthood, inside the pooled rainwater collected in a single epiphyte's leaf structure, never once descending to the ground below.
(B) Epiphytic plants growing on the branches of canopy trees collect fallen leaves, rainwater, and airborne debris in small pockets, forming miniature, self-contained pools many metres above the ground.
(C) An entire community of insects, amphibians, and microorganisms can therefore complete generations of their life cycle within a canopy that a ground-based survey would never detect at all.

Arrange sentences ①–⑤ so that they fit the passage. Which sentence should come fourth?

Behavioural economists distinguish between a decision made in a "hot" emotionally aroused state and the same decision reconsidered in a "cold," calm state.

① People in a hot state consistently underestimate how much their own future judgement will be shaped by emotional arousal, a pattern called the hot-cold empathy gap.
② A person deciding calmly, in a cold state, what to eat at a restaurant next week routinely chooses more modestly than the same person, ravenously hungry, deciding in the moment.
③ This gap has practical consequences: policies and personal commitments designed in a cold state are frequently undermined by decisions made later in a hot state that the earlier, calmer self never anticipated.
④ Because of this gap, commitment devices made deliberately hard to reverse in a cold state — a signed contract, a public pledge — are often more effective than relying on willpower alone in the heat of the moment.
⑤ Neither state, researchers emphasise, gives uniquely accurate access to a person's "true" preference; each simply weighs different, equally real considerations.

Shoppers offered a small, free sample in a supermarket aisle purchase the sampled product at a substantially higher rate than shoppers who walk past the same product with no sample offered, even though the sample itself has no persuasive content whatsoever beyond taste. Researchers attribute much of the effect to a mild, largely unconscious sense of reciprocal obligation: having received something, however small and freely offered, a shopper feels a faint pull to reciprocate, and purchasing becomes the most immediately available way to do so.

Receiving a small free sample can increase a shopper's likelihood of purchasing, largely because of a (A) ________ sense of obligation to (B) ________ something in return.

options.text: (A) conscious (B) refuse
(A) mild, largely unconscious (B) reciprocate
(A) legally binding (B) avoid giving
(A) mild, largely unconscious (B) criticise
(A) conscious (B) forget
